readerTitle: Why paying for what people already love can backfire
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Lepper 외 1973 유치원 그림 실험, 스웨덴 헌혈 실험 2008, Safelite 성과급 2000) + 가상 사례 (컨설팅 회사, 레스토랑)
insight: 보상은 동기를 더해 주기만 하는 것이 아니다. 사람들이 '내가 이 일을 왜 하는가'를 이해하는 방식 자체를 바꾼다.
misconception: 보상을 더하면 동기도 늘어난다. 이미 즐겁게 하는 일에 돈을 얹으면 더 열심히 할 것이다.

sources.text: Lepper, M. R., Greene, D., & Nisbett, R. E. (1973). Undermining children's intrinsic interest with extrinsic reward: A test of the "overjustification" hypothesis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 28(1), 129–137.
Deci, E. L., Koestner, R., & Ryan, R. M. (1999). A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation. Psychological Bulletin, 125(6), 627–668.
Mellström, C., & Johannesson, M. (2008). Crowding out in blood donation: Was Titmuss right? Journal of the European Economic Association, 6(4), 845–863.
Lazear, E. P. (2000). Performance Pay and Productivity. American Economic Review, 90(5), 1346–1361.

factChecks.note: Lepper 외(1973): 그림을 좋아하는 유치원생을 세 집단(보상 예고, 예고 없는 보상, 보상 없음)으로 나눔. 1~2주 뒤 자유 시간 관찰에서 보상을 예고받은 집단만 그림 그리는 시간이 줄었고, 예고 없이 보상받은 집단은 줄지 않았음. 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체적 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.
Mellström & Johannesson(2008): 스웨덴에서 헌혈 검사에 현금을 주자 여성의 참여가 줄었고, 같은 금액을 자선단체에 기부할 수 있게 하자 참여가 회복됨. 남성은 유의미한 차이가 없었음. 카드에는 수치 없이 방향만 적었습니다. 원문으로 확인하세요.
Lazear(2000): Safelite가 시급제에서 개수 기준 성과급으로 바꾼 뒤 생산성이 약 44% 올랐고, 그중 약 절반은 생산적인 직원이 남고 들어온 효과로 분석됨. 수치를 원문으로 확인하세요.
Deci 외(1999) 메타분석: 흥미로운 과제에서 미리 약속된, 과제 수행에 따른 보상이 자유 선택 시간의 내재적 흥미를 낮춤. 예고 없는 보상과 언어적 칭찬은 대체로 해당하지 않음. 카드 문구가 이 범위를 넘지 않는지 확인하세요.
PPL-04-06(인센티브 역효과)과 겹치지 않도록 이 레슨은 내재적·외재적 동기의 구분과 '보상이 일의 의미를 바꾼다'는 관점에 집중하고, 측정 지표 왜곡(게이밍) 같은 내용은 다루지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Kids who loved drawing were promised a prize. Then they drew less.
body: In a 1973 study, psychologists picked preschoolers who already loved to draw. Some were promised a "Good Player" certificate for drawing. They drew, and got their prize.
A week or two later, the markers were back out during free play. The children who had worked for the prize spent less time drawing than the others.

image.label: A child's drawing next to a gold certificate, markers left untouched
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 유치원 책상 위에 아이 그림 한 장과 금색 리본 상장. 옆에 쓰이지 않은 색연필 통이 놓여 있고, 아이는 화면 밖으로 걸어 나가는 뒷모습만 살짝. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your team writes case notes for free. You want more.
body: You run a 40-person consulting firm. A few consultants write short notes on past projects that help colleagues win new clients. Nobody asked them to. They say they enjoy it.
You want more of these notes. What do you do?

options.feedback: You'll likely get more notes at first. But writing them may start to feel like a paid chore, and quality and goodwill can drop once the money is the reason.

options.text: Set a quota: two notes per person each quarter
options.feedback: Everyone contributes, which spreads the load. But a quota turns a chosen task into a required one, and forced notes tend to be thin.

options.text: Protect time for writing and show writers how their notes helped win work
options.feedback: This keeps the reasons they already write, like craft and helping colleagues, and makes them stronger. It costs time, not cash, and grows more slowly.

cards.title: It wasn't the prize. It was the promise.
body: The study had three groups. One was told about the prize in advance. One got the same prize as a surprise. One got nothing.
Only the group that drew *in order to* get the prize lost interest later. The surprise group kept drawing as much as before.
Later reviews of many experiments found a similar pattern for interesting tasks: **rewards promised in advance** for doing the task tended to lower people's interest once the reward was gone.

image.label: Three groups: promised prize, surprise prize, no prize
image.brief: 세 칸 비교 인포그래픽. "Promised prize", "Surprise prize", "No prize". 각 칸에 아이 아이콘과 나중의 그림 그리기 시간을 막대로 표시하되, 첫 칸 막대만 눈에 띄게 짧게. 정확한 수치는 넣지 않음.

cards.title: Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation
body: **Intrinsic motivation** means doing something because the activity itself is rewarding: it's interesting, satisfying or meaningful. **Extrinsic motivation** means doing it for something separate: pay, prizes, praise or avoiding trouble.

Both are real and both work. The twist is how they interact. A promised reward can change the story people tell themselves, from "I do this because I like it" to "I do this because I'm paid." When the reward stops, so does the reason.

cards.title: Paying blood donors, and what fixed it.
body: In a 2008 field experiment in Sweden, people were invited to become blood donors. Some were offered a small cash payment. Among women, the cash offer led to *fewer* sign-ups, not more.
Then researchers let a third group give the same money to a children's charity instead. Sign-ups recovered.
The money itself wasn't the problem. It changed what the act meant. Giving blood went from a kind act to a small, slightly awkward sale.

cards.title: For routine work, extrinsic pay can work very well.
body: This doesn't mean rewards fail. When Safelite, a US auto-glass company, moved installers from hourly pay to pay per windshield, output per worker rose sharply, according to a study by economist Edward Lazear.
Installing windshields is clear, countable work that few people do for the joy of it. There was little intrinsic interest to crowd out.
The useful question isn't "rewards or no rewards?" It's: **why does this person already do this task?**
cards.softwareNote: The same split shows up in software teams. Paying per bug fixed can speed up dull triage work. Paying per internal tool or open-source contribution can turn a passion project into a ticket that someone counts.

cards.title: This is not a reason to pay people less.
body: People need fair pay before any of this matters. Underpaid staff don't feel inspired; they feel used. Pay well enough that money stops being the thing on their mind.

The risk sits in one place: rewards that are promised in advance and tied to doing an activity people already enjoy. Surprise thanks after the fact, and honest praise, usually don't do the same damage.
And people differ. The same task can be a joy to one person and a chore to another.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant kitchen.
body: Your two line cooks love inventing the weekly special. Guests rave, and the specials sell well. You'd like a new special every week instead of every few weeks.
What's your best move?

options.text: Offer $50 for each special that makes the menu, plus a share of its sales
options.feedback: It rewards results, but now the fun part of the job is a sales contest. Cooks may play it safe or start arguing over credit.

options.text: Check their base pay is fair, then give them prep time and share guest feedback
options.feedback: Fair pay takes money off the table, and time plus feedback feeds what they already enjoy. You may not hit one a week, but you keep the spark.

options.text: Leave everything as is, but treat them to a surprise dinner after a great month
options.feedback: A surprise thank-you rarely hurts interest, so it's safe. But it doesn't give them the time they'd need to create more often.

cards.softwareNote: In a software company, the same choice comes up with engineers who build internal tools on their own. Protected time and visible users usually do more than a per-tool bonus.

cards.title: Before you reward a task, ask why people already do it.
body: If they do it for the work itself, protect that reason with fair pay, time and feedback. If it's routine work nobody loves, clear extrinsic rewards can help a lot.
**Try it today:** pick one thing your team does without being asked. Write down why you think they do it, then ask one of them.
